paragraphs: Children in care in Rutland are looked after by Rutland County Council's own fostering service, shown above with the independent agencies that cover the county. The council says that when no carer can be found locally, a child may have to live a long way from school, friends and family, which is why it recruits carers within Rutland.

In October 2024 the council said only 29 per cent of the children in its care were living with mainstream foster carers, and that some children were waiting for a carer or had been placed outside the county because there were not enough local homes. It was looking for people to foster full time and long term, as well as for short stays, single nights and a weekend a month.

To foster with the council you need to be over 21 and have a spare room. There is no set income, and you can be single, married, divorced, living with a partner or in a same-sex relationship, rent or own your home, work or receive benefits, have children or not, and have a disability. Convictions for offences against children rule people out. The council says flexibility with your time and a willingness to care for a child matter most.

The council's process has five steps: an enquiry, a home visit from the team, an application with checks and references, an assessment with an allocated social worker, and approval at a fostering panel. It said in 2024 that this usually takes around six months. Council carers get professional training, financial support and a supervising social worker. The minimum the government sets for 2026-27 outside London and the South East runs from £176 a week for a baby to £267 for a 16 or 17 year old.
Speak to two or three of the services above about the children they need homes for and the support they give.
